title: Kinematics & Newton's Laws
description: Constant-acceleration equations, free fall, projectiles, relative velocity, Newton's laws, friction, inclines, Atwood machines, circular motion and drag.

cards.title: With constant acceleration, which kinematic equation relates $v$, $v_0$, $a$ and the displacement $\Delta x$ without involving time?
cards.body:
$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\,\Delta x$

Use it when **time** is neither given nor asked for.

Why: eliminate $t$ between $v = v_0 + at$ and $\Delta x = v_0t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.
Watch out: like every constant-acceleration equation, it fails when $a$ varies (for example, with air drag).
cards.searchQuery: kinematic equation without time v squared

cards.title: Near Earth's surface, what is the standard magnitude of the free-fall acceleration $g$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$ to 3 significant figures?
cards.body:
$g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, directed downward.

Near Earth's surface it is the same for every object, whatever its mass, when air resistance is negligible.

Tip: with up as positive, $a = -g$ for the whole flight, rising or falling.
Watch out: many problems round to $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$; use whatever value the problem states.
cards.searchQuery: standard acceleration of gravity 9.81 m/s2

cards.title: A ball is thrown straight up. At its highest point, what are its velocity and its acceleration? (Neglect air resistance.)
cards.body:
Velocity $0$; acceleration still $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ downward.

The acceleration is the same at every instant of the flight, rising, at the top and falling.

Watch out: zero velocity does **not** mean zero acceleration. If $a$ were $0$ at the top, the ball would hover there.
cards.searchQuery: acceleration at top of vertical throw

cards.title: In projectile motion with no air resistance, how does the horizontal component of the velocity change during the flight?
cards.body:
It doesn't change: $v_x = v_0\cos\theta$ stays constant ($\theta$ is the launch angle).

Gravity acts only vertically, so $a_x = 0$ and $a_y = -g$.

Key idea: at the peak the velocity is not zero; it equals $v_0\cos\theta$, pointing horizontally.
cards.searchQuery: projectile motion horizontal velocity constant

cards.title: A ball is launched from level ground at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. How long is it in the air, in seconds to 3 significant figures? (No drag; $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$2.04\,\mathrm{s}$

$T = \dfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g} = \dfrac{2(20)(0.50)}{9.8}$. Only the **vertical** motion sets the time.

Why: the vertical velocity of $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ reaches zero after $1.02\,\mathrm{s}$, and the fall back down takes just as long.
Watch out: this formula is valid only when the projectile lands at its launch height.
cards.searchQuery: projectile time of flight 2 v sin theta over g

cards.title: On level ground (no air resistance), a projectile launched at $30^\circ$ has range $R$. At what other launch angle, in degrees, does the same speed also give range $R$?
cards.body:
$60^\circ$

$R = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$, and $\sin 60^\circ = \sin 120^\circ$, so **complementary angles** ($\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$) give equal ranges.

Key idea: the maximum range comes at $45^\circ$, where $\sin 2\theta = 1$.
cards.searchQuery: complementary launch angles equal range projectile

cards.title: A boat points straight across a river at $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ relative to the water; the current is $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its speed relative to the shore, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$

Velocities add as vectors: $\vec{v}_{\text{boat/shore}} = \vec{v}_{\text{boat/water}} + \vec{v}_{\text{water/shore}}$. The parts are perpendicular, so the speed is $\sqrt{3.0^2 + 4.0^2} = 5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Watch out: the current carries the boat downstream, but the crossing time is still the river's width divided by $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
cards.searchQuery: boat river current relative velocity vector addition

cards.title: A hockey puck slides across frictionless ice at constant velocity. What is the net force on it, in newtons?
cards.body:
Zero.

Newton's first law: constant velocity means $\vec{a} = 0$, so $\sum\vec{F} = 0$. This holds in inertial reference frames.

Watch out: no force is needed to *keep* an object moving; a net force *changes* its velocity.
cards.searchQuery: Newton first law constant velocity net force zero

cards.title: Newton's third-law force pairs are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Why don't they cancel each other out?
cards.body:
They act on **different bodies**, and only forces on the same body add up to its net force.

A third-law pair is always the same type of force (for example, both gravitational).

Watch out: a book's weight and the table's normal force on it both act on the book, so they are **not** a third-law pair.
cards.searchQuery: Newton third law action reaction pairs do not cancel

cards.title: A $60\,\mathrm{kg}$ person stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. What does the scale read, in newtons? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$708\,\mathrm{N}$ ($\approx 710\,\mathrm{N}$), more than $mg = 588\,\mathrm{N}$.

With up positive, $N - mg = ma$, so $N = m(g + a) = (60)(9.8 + 2.0)$.

Why: only the **acceleration** matters, not the direction of motion. Moving down while slowing at $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ gives the same reading.
Example: in free fall ($a = -g$) the scale reads $0$.
cards.searchQuery: elevator apparent weight scale reading accelerating upward

cards.title: A block of mass $m$ sits on a ramp inclined at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. What is the component of its weight parallel to the ramp?
cards.body:
$mg\sin\theta$, pointing down the slope.

The perpendicular component is $mg\cos\theta$, balanced by the normal force ($N = mg\cos\theta$ if nothing else pushes perpendicular to the ramp).

Tip: check the limits. $\theta = 0$ gives no downslope pull; $\theta = 90^\circ$ gives all of $mg$.
cards.searchQuery: weight component parallel to incline mg sin theta

cards.title: A crate on a floor has $\mu_s = 0.50$ and normal force $100\,\mathrm{N}$. You push it horizontally with $30\,\mathrm{N}$ and it stays put. What is the friction force, in newtons?
cards.body:
$30\,\mathrm{N}$, opposing your push.

Static friction is only as large as needed, up to $f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N = 50\,\mathrm{N}$.

Watch out: $\mu_s N$ is the **maximum**, not the actual value.
Why: once the crate slides, kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$ takes over (usually $\mu_k < \mu_s$).
cards.searchQuery: static friction less than maximum mu N crate pushed

cards.title: In an ideal Atwood machine with masses $m_1 > m_2$ (massless string, frictionless massless pulley), what is the magnitude of the acceleration?
cards.body:
$a = \dfrac{(m_1 - m_2)\,g}{m_1 + m_2}$

The net driving force $(m_1 - m_2)g$ accelerates the **total** mass $m_1 + m_2$.

Watch out: the tension $T = \dfrac{2m_1m_2\,g}{m_1 + m_2}$ lies between $m_2g$ and $m_1g$; it is not simply the heavier weight.
cards.searchQuery: Atwood machine acceleration formula

cards.title: An object moves at constant speed $v$ around a circle of radius $r$. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?
cards.body:
$a = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$, directed toward the center.

The speed is constant but the velocity keeps changing direction, so the object accelerates. An equivalent form is $a = \omega^2 r$.

Example: $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ on a $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ radius gives $a = 20\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
cards.searchQuery: centripetal acceleration v squared over r

cards.title: A car rounds a flat, unbanked curve at constant speed. Which force provides the centripetal force?
cards.body:
**Static friction** from the road on the tires, pointing toward the center of the curve.

It is static because the tires don't slide sideways. The maximum speed is $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$.

Watch out: centripetal force is never an extra force on a free-body diagram; it is the name for the net inward force.
cards.searchQuery: car flat curve centripetal force static friction

cards.title: An object of mass $m$ falls through air with drag force $D = \tfrac{1}{2}C\rho Av^2$. What is its terminal speed?
cards.body:
$v_t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mg}{C\rho A}}$

At terminal speed, drag balances weight: $\tfrac{1}{2}C\rho Av_t^2 = mg$. The net force and the acceleration are zero.

Example: a heavier object of the same size and shape falls faster. In a vacuum there is no terminal speed.
cards.searchQuery: terminal speed quadratic drag formula

cards.title: A runner completes one full lap of a $400\,\mathrm{m}$ track, ending where she started. What is her displacement, in meters?
cards.body:
$0$; the distance she covered is $400\,\mathrm{m}$.

**Displacement** is the change in position, $\Delta x = x_f - x_i$, a vector. **Distance** is the total path length, a scalar that never decreases.

Key idea: her average velocity for the lap is zero, but her average speed is not.
cards.searchQuery: displacement versus distance full lap zero

cards.title: A car drives $60\,\mathrm{km}$ at $30\,\mathrm{km/h}$, then returns the same $60\,\mathrm{km}$ at $60\,\mathrm{km/h}$. What is its average speed for the round trip, in $\mathrm{km/h}$?
cards.body:
$40\,\mathrm{km/h}$, not $45\,\mathrm{km/h}$.

Average speed is total distance over total time: $120\,\mathrm{km}$ in $2.0\,\mathrm{h} + 1.0\,\mathrm{h} = 3.0\,\mathrm{h}$.

Why: the car spends more time at the lower speed, so the average is weighted toward it.
Example: its average velocity for the round trip is zero.
cards.searchQuery: average speed round trip different speeds harmonic

cards.title: How is instantaneous velocity defined in terms of the position function $x(t)$?
cards.body:
$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$, the limit of $\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ as $\Delta t \to 0$.

Graphically, it is the **slope of the tangent line** to the position-time graph at that instant.

Key idea: speed is the magnitude of this velocity.
cards.searchQuery: instantaneous velocity derivative of position

cards.title: Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity. What is it in terms of the position function $x(t)$?
cards.body:
$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}$

It is the slope of the velocity-time graph, and its sign gives the concavity of the position-time graph.

Tip: going the other way, integrate: $v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t a\,dt'$.
cards.searchQuery: acceleration second derivative of position

cards.title: A particle's position is $x(t) = 3t^2 - 4t$, with $x$ in meters and $t$ in seconds. What is its velocity at $t = 2.0\,\mathrm{s}$, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$

Differentiate: $v(t) = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 6t - 4$, so $v(2.0) = 12 - 4 = 8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The acceleration is a constant $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Watch out: $x(2.0)/2.0 = 2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is the average velocity since $t = 0$, not the instantaneous velocity.
cards.searchQuery: velocity from position function derivative

cards.title: On a velocity–time graph, what does the signed area between the curve and the time axis represent?
cards.body:
The **displacement**, $\Delta x = \int v\,dt$.

Area below the axis counts as negative (motion in the negative direction). For the total distance traveled, count every area as positive.

Key idea: the slope of the same graph is the acceleration.
cards.searchQuery: area under velocity time graph displacement

cards.title: On an acceleration–time graph, what does the area under the curve over an interval represent?
cards.body:
The **change in velocity**, $\Delta v = \int a\,dt$.

It gives only the change; to find the velocity itself you also need its initial value.

Key idea: the pattern repeats one level down: the area under a $v$-$t$ graph is the change in position.
cards.searchQuery: area under acceleration time graph change in velocity

cards.title: An object's position–time graph is a parabola that opens upward. What can you conclude about its acceleration?
cards.body:
The acceleration is constant and positive.

$x = x_0 + v_0t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ is a parabola in $t$; opening upward (concave up) means $a > 0$.

Why: the slope at each point is the instantaneous velocity. It is zero at the vertex, where the object momentarily stops and reverses direction.
cards.searchQuery: position time graph parabola constant acceleration

cards.title: An object has negative velocity and negative acceleration. Is it speeding up or slowing down?
cards.body:
**Speeding up.**

An object speeds up when $v$ and $a$ have the **same sign** and slows down when their signs are opposite.

Watch out: negative acceleration doesn't by itself mean slowing down; it depends on the direction of motion.
cards.searchQuery: speeding up or slowing down sign of velocity and acceleration

cards.title: For constant acceleration $a$, what is the velocity $v$ at time $t$ in terms of the initial velocity $v_0$?
cards.body:
$v = v_0 + at$

It follows from the definition $a = \Delta v/\Delta t$ when $a$ is constant.

Key idea: the $v$-$t$ graph is a straight line with slope $a$ and intercept $v_0$.
cards.searchQuery: constant acceleration velocity equation v = v0 + at

cards.title: For constant acceleration, what is the displacement $\Delta x$ after time $t$, in terms of $v_0$, $a$ and $t$?
cards.body:
$\Delta x = v_0t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$

It is the area under the straight-line $v$-$t$ graph: a rectangle $v_0t$ plus a triangle $\tfrac{1}{2}(at)t$.

Tip: if the final velocity $v$ is known instead of $v_0$, use $\Delta x = vt - \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.
cards.searchQuery: constant acceleration displacement equation v0 t plus half a t squared

cards.title: Under constant acceleration, how is the average velocity over an interval related to the initial and final velocities $v_0$ and $v$?
cards.body:
$\bar{v} = \dfrac{v_0 + v}{2}$, so $\Delta x = \dfrac{v_0 + v}{2}\,t$.

This works because the velocity changes linearly in time.

Watch out: it is valid only for **constant acceleration**. Otherwise the average velocity is $\Delta x/\Delta t$, which generally differs from the mean of the endpoint velocities.
cards.searchQuery: average velocity constant acceleration mean of initial and final

cards.title: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to $27\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in $9.0\,\mathrm{s}$. What is its acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$?
cards.body:
$3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$

$a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{27\,\mathrm{m/s} - 0}{9.0\,\mathrm{s}}$.

Tip: the units $(\mathrm{m/s})/\mathrm{s}$ tell the story: the velocity grows by $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ every second.
cards.searchQuery: acceleration from change in velocity over time car

cards.title: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ for $5.0\,\mathrm{s}$. How far does it travel, in meters?
cards.body:
$50\,\mathrm{m}$

$\Delta x = v_0t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(4.0)(5.0)^2$.

Tip: check with the average velocity. The car ends at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$, averages $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $(10\,\mathrm{m/s})(5.0\,\mathrm{s}) = 50\,\mathrm{m}$.
cards.searchQuery: distance traveled uniform acceleration from rest

cards.title: A car moving at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ brakes with a constant deceleration of $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. How far does it travel before stopping, in meters?
cards.body:
$40\,\mathrm{m}$

No time is given or asked for, so use $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\,\Delta x$: $0 = 20^2 + 2(-5.0)\,\Delta x$.

Watch out: with the motion taken as positive, the braking acceleration is **negative**.
Example: stopping takes $v_0/|a| = 4.0\,\mathrm{s}$.
cards.searchQuery: braking distance constant deceleration kinematics

cards.title: A driver moving at $25\,\mathrm{m/s}$ has a $0.80\,\mathrm{s}$ reaction time before braking. How far does the car travel during the reaction time, in meters?
cards.body:
$20\,\mathrm{m}$

Until the brakes engage, the car keeps its constant velocity: $d = vt = (25)(0.80)$.

Key idea: total stopping distance is the reaction distance (proportional to $v$) plus the braking distance (proportional to $v^2$).
cards.searchQuery: driver reaction time distance traveled constant velocity

cards.title: A speeder passes a parked police car at a constant $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. At that instant the police car starts from rest at $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. How many seconds until it catches up?
cards.body:
$20\,\mathrm{s}$

Set the positions equal: $\tfrac{1}{2}(2.0)t^2 = 20t$, so $t = 20\,\mathrm{s}$ (the other root, $t = 0$, is the start).

Why: over the same time the two have equal average velocities, so the police car's final speed is twice the speeder's: $40\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
cards.searchQuery: police car catch up speeder constant acceleration equal positions

cards.title: A particle starts from rest with acceleration $a(t) = 6t$ (in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$, with $t$ in seconds). What is its speed at $t = 2.0\,\mathrm{s}$, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$12\,\mathrm{m/s}$

Integrate: $v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t 6t'\,dt' = 3t^2$, so $v(2.0) = 12\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Watch out: $v = at$ holds only for constant acceleration; here it would wrongly give $(12)(2.0) = 24\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
cards.searchQuery: velocity from acceleration function integrate

cards.title: A stone is dropped from rest off a $45\,\mathrm{m}$ cliff. How long does it take to reach the ground, in seconds to 2 significant figures? (No drag; $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$3.0\,\mathrm{s}$

From $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$: $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(45)}{9.8}} \approx 3.03\,\mathrm{s}$.

Key idea: fall time grows only as $\sqrt{h}$; four times the height takes twice as long.
cards.searchQuery: free fall time dropped from cliff sqrt 2h over g

cards.title: A ball is dropped from rest $20\,\mathrm{m}$ above the ground. How fast is it moving just before impact, in $\mathrm{m/s}$ to 2 significant figures? (No drag; $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ ($19.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$).

With no time given, use $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2gh$: $v = \sqrt{2(9.8)(20)}$.

Key idea: doubling the height multiplies the impact speed by only $\sqrt{2}$, and the ball's mass doesn't enter.
cards.searchQuery: free fall impact speed sqrt 2gh dropped ball

cards.title: How far does an object dropped from rest fall in its first $2.0\,\mathrm{s}$, in meters to 3 significant figures? (No drag; $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$19.6\,\mathrm{m}$

$d = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(2.0)^2$. It is then moving at $gt = 19.6\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Example: distances fallen in successive seconds go as $1 : 3 : 5 : 7$ ($4.9$, $14.7$, $24.5$, $34.3\,\mathrm{m}$).
cards.searchQuery: free fall distance after 2 seconds from rest

cards.title: A ball is thrown straight up at $14\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How high does it rise above the launch point, in meters? (No drag; $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$10\,\mathrm{m}$

At the top $v = 0$, so $0 = v_0^2 - 2gh$ gives $h = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2g} = \dfrac{14^2}{2(9.8)}$.

Example: it gets there after $v_0/g \approx 1.4\,\mathrm{s}$.
cards.searchQuery: maximum height vertical throw v0 squared over 2g

cards.title: A ball thrown straight up at speed $v_0$ comes back down to its launch height. What is its speed there, with no air resistance?
cards.body:
$v_0$, the launch speed, now directed downward.

The rise and fall are mirror images: at each height the speed is the same going up and coming down, and the up and down trips take equal times.

Watch out: air drag breaks the symmetry and makes the return speed smaller.
cards.searchQuery: ball thrown up returns with same speed no air resistance

cards.title: A velocity of magnitude $v$ points at angle $\theta$ above the $+x$ axis. What are its $x$- and $y$-components?
cards.body:
$v_x = v\cos\theta$ and $v_y = v\sin\theta$.

Cosine goes with the side **adjacent** to $\theta$. To go back: $v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$ and $\tan\theta = v_y/v_x$ (check the quadrant).

Watch out: if the angle is measured from the vertical instead, the roles of sine and cosine swap.
cards.searchQuery: vector components cosine sine velocity angle

cards.title: A plane flies $200\,\mathrm{km}$ in a straight line at $30^\circ$ north of east. How far north of its starting point does it end up, in kilometers?
cards.body:
$100\,\mathrm{km}$

The angle is measured from east, so the northward component is $d\sin 30^\circ = (200)(0.50)$. The eastward component is $d\cos 30^\circ \approx 173\,\mathrm{km}$.

Tip: check with $\sqrt{100^2 + 173^2} \approx 200$.
cards.searchQuery: north of east displacement component sine

cards.title: One bullet is fired horizontally and another is dropped from the same height at the same instant. Which hits level ground first? (No air resistance.)
cards.body:
Neither: they land **at the same time**.

Horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Both bullets start with zero vertical velocity and fall with the same acceleration $g$.

Key idea: the fired bullet just covers horizontal distance while it falls.
cards.searchQuery: horizontally fired bullet and dropped bullet land together

cards.title: A ball rolls off a $1.25\,\mathrm{m}$ high table at $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How far from the table's edge does it land, in meters to 2 significant figures? (No drag; $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$1.5\,\mathrm{m}$

The fall time comes from the vertical motion alone: $t = \sqrt{2h/g} = \sqrt{2(1.25)/9.8} \approx 0.505\,\mathrm{s}$.

Why: horizontally the speed stays constant, so $x = v_0t = (3.0)(0.505) \approx 1.52\,\mathrm{m}$.
cards.searchQuery: horizontal projectile off table landing distance

cards.title: What is the range of a projectile launched at speed $v_0$ and angle $\theta$ above the horizontal that lands at its launch height? (No air resistance.)
cards.body:
$R = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$

It is the horizontal speed $v_0\cos\theta$ times the flight time $\dfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}$, simplified with $2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta$.

Tip: doubling the launch speed quadruples the range.
cards.searchQuery: projectile range formula v0 squared sin 2 theta over g

cards.title: On level ground with no air resistance, what launch angle gives a projectile its maximum range, in degrees?
cards.body:
$45^\circ$

$R = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$ is largest when $\sin 2\theta = 1$, giving $R_{\max} = v_0^2/g$.

Watch out: with air resistance, or when landing below the launch point, the best angle is somewhat less than $45^\circ$.
cards.searchQuery: maximum range launch angle 45 degrees projectile

cards.title: A ball is kicked from level ground at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. What maximum height does it reach, in meters to 2 significant figures? (No drag; $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$5.1\,\mathrm{m}$

$H = \dfrac{(v_0\sin\theta)^2}{2g} = \dfrac{(10\,\mathrm{m/s})^2}{2(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})} \approx 5.10\,\mathrm{m}$.

Key idea: only the vertical component matters; a ball thrown straight up at $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ rises just as high.
cards.searchQuery: projectile maximum height vertical component

cards.title: During a projectile's flight (no air resistance), what is the direction of its acceleration, including at the peak?
cards.body:
Straight down, with magnitude $g$, at every point of the flight.

The velocity changes direction along the parabola, but the acceleration doesn't.

Example: at the peak the velocity is horizontal and the acceleration is perpendicular to it, still $g$ downward.
cards.searchQuery: projectile acceleration direction downward at peak

cards.title: Why is the path of a projectile (no air resistance) a parabola?
cards.body:
$x$ changes **linearly** with time while $y$ is **quadratic** in time.

Eliminating $t = x/v_{0x}$ from $y = v_{0y}t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ gives $y = \dfrac{v_{0y}}{v_{0x}}x - \dfrac{g}{2v_{0x}^2}x^2$, a downward-opening parabola.

Key idea: constant horizontal velocity plus constant vertical acceleration.
cards.searchQuery: why projectile path is a parabola

cards.title: A projectile is launched from level ground at speed $v_0$ and angle $\theta$. With what speed and direction does it land? (No air resistance.)
cards.body:
Speed $v_0$, at angle $\theta$ below the horizontal.

The horizontal component $v_0\cos\theta$ is unchanged and the vertical component has reversed, to $-v_0\sin\theta$.

Key idea: the path is symmetric about the peak (for landing at launch height).
cards.searchQuery: projectile landing speed and angle same as launch

cards.title: Two projectiles launched from level ground reach the same maximum height but have different ranges. Which stays in the air longer? (No air resistance.)
cards.body:
Neither: their flight times are **equal**.

The flight time depends only on the vertical motion, $T = \dfrac{2v_{0y}}{g}$, and the peak height $\dfrac{v_{0y}^2}{2g}$ fixes $v_{0y}$.

Why: the longer-range projectile just has a larger horizontal velocity.
cards.searchQuery: same maximum height same flight time projectiles

cards.title: A plane flying level at constant velocity drops a package. Ignoring air resistance, where is the package relative to the plane as it falls?
cards.body:
Directly below the plane the whole time.

The package keeps the plane's horizontal velocity (Newton's first law), so both cover the same horizontal distance.

Example: from the ground it traces a parabola; from the plane it falls straight down.
cards.searchQuery: package dropped from moving plane stays below plane

cards.title: A dart is aimed straight at a monkey hanging from a branch, and the monkey lets go just as the dart is fired. Does the dart hit it? (No air resistance.)
cards.body:
**Yes**, as long as the dart reaches the monkey's horizontal position before either hits the ground.

At every instant both have fallen the same distance, $\tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, below where they would be without gravity.

Why: the dart drops below its aim line exactly as much as the monkey drops below the branch.
cards.searchQuery: monkey and hunter problem dart aimed at falling monkey

cards.title: A passenger on a train moving at constant velocity tosses a ball straight up (relative to herself). Where does it land, ignoring air resistance?
cards.body:
Back in her hand.

The ball shares the train's horizontal velocity and keeps it while in the air, so ball and passenger stay level horizontally. All inertial frames are equivalent.

Watch out: if the train speeds up meanwhile, the ball lands behind her.
cards.searchQuery: ball tossed up in train moving constant velocity inertial frame

cards.title: A boat that moves at $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ relative to the water crosses a river flowing at $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ along a path straight across. What is its speed relative to the shore, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$

The boat must head partly upstream so that $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ of its water-relative velocity cancels the current, leaving $\sqrt{5.0^2 - 3.0^2} = 4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ straight across.

Example: its heading is $\sin^{-1}(3/5) \approx 37^\circ$ upstream of straight across.
Watch out: if the current were faster than the boat, a straight crossing would be impossible.
cards.searchQuery: boat crossing river straight across heading upstream speed

cards.title: Car A drives east at $25\,\mathrm{m/s}$ toward car B, which drives west at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is A's speed relative to B, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$45\,\mathrm{m/s}$

$\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B = (+25) - (-20) = +45\,\mathrm{m/s}$, that is, east.

Tip: head-on, the speeds add; moving the same way, they subtract.
Watch out: this Galilean rule fails near the speed of light.
cards.searchQuery: relative velocity head on cars add speeds

cards.title: An object moves at constant speed around a circle of radius $r$, completing one revolution in period $T$. What is its speed?
cards.body:
$v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$

One circumference per period. Combined with $a = v^2/r$, the centripetal acceleration is $a = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2}$.

Tip: with frequency $f = 1/T$, $v = 2\pi rf$.
cards.searchQuery: circular motion speed from period 2 pi r over T

cards.title: A car speeds up while rounding a curve. Besides the centripetal component $v^2/r$, what other component does its acceleration have?
cards.body:
A **tangential** component, $a_t = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$, along the velocity.

The two components are perpendicular, so the magnitude is $a = \sqrt{a_t^2 + (v^2/r)^2}$.

Key idea: the tangential part changes the speed; the centripetal part changes the direction.
cards.searchQuery: nonuniform circular motion tangential acceleration

cards.title: Which property of an object measures its inertia, its resistance to changes in velocity?
cards.body:
Its **mass**.

For a given net force, $a = F/m$, so a larger mass changes its velocity less. Mass is a scalar measured in kilograms and is the same everywhere.

Watch out: weight, the gravitational force $mg$, depends on location; mass does not.
cards.searchQuery: mass measures inertia resistance to change in velocity

cards.title: Write Newton's second law for an object of constant mass $m$.
cards.body:
$\sum\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$

It is a vector equation: the acceleration points along the net force, and it holds for each component separately ($\sum F_x = ma_x$, and so on).

Watch out: only forces acting **on** the object count.
cards.searchQuery: Newton second law net force equals mass times acceleration

cards.title: Express one newton in SI base units.
cards.body:
$1\,\mathrm{N} = 1\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2}$

It is the net force that gives a $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass an acceleration of $1\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, straight from $F = ma$.

Example: a medium apple weighs about $1\,\mathrm{N}$.
cards.searchQuery: newton unit SI base units kg m per s squared

cards.title: An astronaut has a mass of $80\,\mathrm{kg}$ on Earth. What is her mass on the Moon, where $g$ is about one-sixth as large, in kilograms?
cards.body:
$80\,\mathrm{kg}$, unchanged.

Mass measures the amount of inertia and doesn't depend on location.

Example: her weight $mg$ drops to about one-sixth: roughly $130\,\mathrm{N}$ instead of $784\,\mathrm{N}$.
cards.searchQuery: mass versus weight on the moon astronaut

cards.title: A $4.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless surface is pulled east with $20\,\mathrm{N}$ and west with $8.0\,\mathrm{N}$. What is the magnitude of its acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$?
cards.body:
$3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, toward the east.

Add the forces as vectors first: $\sum F = 20 - 8.0 = 12\,\mathrm{N}$ east. Then $a = \dfrac{\sum F}{m} = \dfrac{12}{4.0}$.

Watch out: don't divide just one of the forces by the mass.
cards.searchQuery: net force opposing pulls acceleration block F = ma

cards.title: In a free-body diagram for one object, which forces do you draw?
cards.body:
Only the **external forces** acting on that object.

Leave out forces the object exerts on other things. Each force needs an identifiable source: Earth, a rope, a surface and so on.

Watch out: don't add 'net force', 'centripetal force' or '$ma$' as extra arrows; those are results, not forces.
cards.searchQuery: free body diagram which forces to draw

cards.title: You push straight down with $10\,\mathrm{N}$ on a $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ book resting on a table. What normal force does the table exert on the book, in newtons? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$29.6\,\mathrm{N}$

The book doesn't accelerate, so $N - mg - F = 0$ and $N = 19.6 + 10 = 29.6\,\mathrm{N}$.

Watch out: the normal force equals $mg$ only when nothing else pushes perpendicular to the surface. It is whatever force the surface must supply.
cards.searchQuery: normal force book pushed down on table

cards.title: Earth pulls a falling apple down with a $1.0\,\mathrm{N}$ gravitational force. How large is the gravitational force of the apple on Earth, in newtons?
cards.body:
$1.0\,\mathrm{N}$, directed up toward the apple.

Newton's third law: the two forces of an interaction are always equal in size and opposite in direction.

Why: Earth's acceleration is negligible only because its mass is enormous ($a = F/m$), not because the force is smaller.
cards.searchQuery: Newton third law apple pulls Earth equal force

cards.title: What does treating a rope as massless let you assume about its tension?
cards.body:
The tension is the **same all along the rope**, even while it accelerates.

For any segment, $T_2 - T_1 = m_{\text{seg}}\,a$; with zero mass the two ends must pull equally.

Tip: an ideal (massless, frictionless) pulley changes the rope's direction but not its tension.
cards.searchQuery: massless rope same tension ideal pulley

cards.title: Two people pull on opposite ends of a rope, each with a $100\,\mathrm{N}$ force, and nothing moves. What is the tension in the rope, in newtons?
cards.body:
$100\,\mathrm{N}$, not $200\,\mathrm{N}$ or $0$.

Tension is the force the rope exerts at either end.

Example: it is the same as tying one end to a wall and pulling with $100\,\mathrm{N}$: the wall pulls back with $100\,\mathrm{N}$, just as the second person does.
cards.searchQuery: tug of war rope tension equal pulls

cards.title: A $10\,\mathrm{kg}$ sign hangs from two ropes, each at $60^\circ$ from the vertical. What is the tension in each rope, in newtons? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$98\,\mathrm{N}$, as large as the sign's whole weight.

The horizontal components cancel; vertically, $2T\cos 60^\circ = mg$, so $T = \dfrac{98\,\mathrm{N}}{2(0.50)}$.

Watch out: the flatter the ropes, the larger the tension; perfectly horizontal ropes could never hold the sign up.
cards.searchQuery: sign hung from two ropes tension angle from vertical

cards.title: What is an inertial reference frame?
cards.body:
A frame in which **Newton's first law** holds: an object with zero net force moves at constant velocity.

Any frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial.

Watch out: accelerating or rotating frames are not; using Newton's laws in them requires fictitious forces, such as the centrifugal force.
cards.searchQuery: inertial reference frame definition

cards.title: An elevator descends at a constant $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What does a scale under a $70\,\mathrm{kg}$ passenger read, in newtons? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$686\,\mathrm{N}$, exactly the passenger's weight $mg$.

Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so $N - mg = 0$.

Watch out: the $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is a distractor. Speed and direction of motion don't change the reading; only acceleration does.
cards.searchQuery: elevator constant velocity scale reading weight

cards.title: On a frictionless floor, a $20\,\mathrm{N}$ push on a $3.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block shoves a $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block ahead of it. What force does the first block exert on the second, in newtons?
cards.body:
$5.0\,\mathrm{N}$

Treat both blocks as one system first: $a = \dfrac{20}{4.0} = 5.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The only horizontal force on the $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block is the contact force, so $F = (1.0)(5.0)$.

Watch out: the push isn't passed on undiminished; part of it accelerates the first block.
cards.searchQuery: contact force between two pushed blocks frictionless

cards.title: A $5.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless table is tied over an ideal pulley to a hanging $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block. What is their acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$2.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$

Only the hanging block's weight drives the system, and it must accelerate both blocks: $a = \dfrac{m_2g}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{(2.0)(9.8)}{7.0}$.

Why: the tension, $T = m_1a = 14\,\mathrm{N}$, is less than the hanging weight ($19.6\,\mathrm{N}$); otherwise the hanging block couldn't accelerate downward.
cards.searchQuery: block on table connected to hanging block over pulley acceleration

cards.title: A block slides down a frictionless incline at angle $\theta$. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?
cards.body:
$a = g\sin\theta$, down the slope, whatever the mass.

The net force along the incline is $mg\sin\theta$; the normal force cancels the perpendicular part of gravity.

Example: at $30^\circ$, $a = g/2 = 4.9\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
cards.searchQuery: frictionless incline acceleration g sin theta

cards.title: A $10\,\mathrm{kg}$ box rests on a $30^\circ$ incline. What is the normal force on it, in newtons to 3 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$84.9\,\mathrm{N}$

$N = mg\cos\theta = (10)(9.8)\cos 30^\circ$. It is less than the weight ($98\,\mathrm{N}$) because the surface balances only the perpendicular component of gravity.

Watch out: mixing up $\sin$ and $\cos$ here is the classic incline mistake.
cards.searchQuery: normal force on incline mg cos theta

cards.title: What is the magnitude of the kinetic friction force on a sliding object, in terms of the normal force $N$ and the coefficient $\mu_k$?
cards.body:
$f_k = \mu_k N$

It points opposite to the object's motion relative to the surface. The coefficient $\mu_k$ is a unitless number set by the two surfaces.

Watch out: $N$ is the **normal force**, which is not always $mg$ (on a slope or with an angled push it differs).
Tip: for a given pair of surfaces, $\mu_k$ is usually smaller than $\mu_s$.
cards.searchQuery: kinetic friction force formula mu N

cards.title: A $20\,\mathrm{kg}$ box slides on a level floor with $\mu_k = 0.30$. What is the kinetic friction force, in newtons to 3 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$58.8\,\mathrm{N}$

On a level floor with no vertical push, $N = mg = (20)(9.8) = 196\,\mathrm{N}$, so $f_k = \mu_k N = (0.30)(196)$.

Watch out: the speed of the box does not matter in this model; friction is not proportional to velocity.
cards.searchQuery: kinetic friction force numeric level floor mu k

cards.title: In the standard friction model, how does the kinetic friction on a box change if you turn it onto a smaller face?
cards.body:
It **doesn't change**.

The model says $f_k = \mu_k N$, and neither $\mu_k$ nor $N$ depends on the contact area.

Watch out: this is an approximation for dry solids; it fails for sticky or soft surfaces such as racing tires.
cards.searchQuery: friction independent of contact area

cards.title: A block rests on a rough incline of angle $\theta$ with static coefficient $\mu_s$. Which relation holds at the angle where it just begins to slide?
cards.body:
$\tan\theta = \mu_s$

At the threshold, $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s N = \mu_s\,mg\cos\theta$. The mass cancels.

Tip: a block stays put whenever $\tan\theta \le \mu_s$, so measuring the angle where it slips gives $\mu_s$ directly.
Watch out: the block's weight and mass never enter this threshold.
cards.searchQuery: incline angle block begins to slip tan theta equals mu s

cards.title: A block on an incline has $\mu_s = 0.75$. At what incline angle does it just begin to slip, in degrees to 3 significant figures?
cards.body:
$36.9^\circ$

Use $\tan\theta = \mu_s$, so $\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.75)$.

Example: $\tan 37^\circ \approx 0.75$, consistent with the familiar 3-4-5 triangle.
cards.searchQuery: angle of incline block slips mu s 0.75 arctan

cards.title: A block slides down an incline of angle $\theta$ with kinetic coefficient $\mu_k$. What is its acceleration down the slope?
cards.body:
$a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$

Along the slope: $mg\sin\theta - \mu_k\,mg\cos\theta = ma$. The mass cancels.

Why: the normal force is $mg\cos\theta$, so friction is $\mu_k mg\cos\theta$.
Watch out: this applies only if $\tan\theta > \mu_k$; otherwise the block decelerates once sliding (and stops).
cards.searchQuery: sliding down incline with friction acceleration formula

cards.title: A block slides down a $30^\circ$ incline with $\mu_k = 0.20$. What is its acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$ to 2 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$3.2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$

$a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta) = 9.8\,(0.500 - 0.20\times 0.866) = 9.8\times 0.327$.

Tip: compare with the frictionless value $g\sin 30^\circ = 4.9\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$; friction should reduce it.
cards.searchQuery: incline friction acceleration numeric 30 degrees mu 0.20

cards.title: A rope pulls a crate of mass $m$ along a floor with tension $T$ at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. What is the normal force on the crate?
cards.body:
$N = mg - T\sin\theta$

The vertical part of the pull, $T\sin\theta$, helps support the crate, so the floor pushes less.

Why: less normal force means less friction, which is one reason pulling upward at a small angle is easier than pulling horizontally.
Watch out: pushing downward at an angle does the opposite and increases $N$.
cards.searchQuery: normal force when pulling at an angle above horizontal

cards.title: A frictionless road banked at angle $\theta$ has radius $r$. At what speed can a car take the curve with no friction needed?
cards.body:
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}$, so $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$.

Only gravity and the normal force act. The normal force's horizontal component, $N\sin\theta$, supplies the centripetal force $mv^2/r$, and its vertical component balances weight: $N\cos\theta = mg$.

Tip: divide the two equations to get $\tan\theta = v^2/(rg)$; the mass cancels.
cards.searchQuery: banked curve ideal speed frictionless tan theta

cards.title: A bucket of water is swung in a vertical circle of radius $r$. What minimum speed at the top keeps the water in contact with the bucket?
cards.body:
$v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}$

At the top, both gravity and the bucket's push point toward the center. The limiting case is zero normal force, so $mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

Watch out: the water doesn't need an outward "force" to stay in; slower than $\sqrt{gr}$, it would fall away from the circular path.
cards.searchQuery: minimum speed top of vertical circle sqrt gr

cards.title: A $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ ball on a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$ at a constant $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the net inward force, in newtons?
cards.body:
$36\,\mathrm{N}$

$F = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{(2.0)(3.0)^2}{0.50}$.

Why: the net inward force equals mass times centripetal acceleration; here the string's tension provides it.
Tip: doubling the speed would quadruple the force.
cards.searchQuery: centripetal force numeric mass v squared over r

cards.title: A car of mass $m$ crosses the top of a circular hill of radius $r$ at speed $v$. What is the normal force from the road at the top?
cards.body:
$N = m\left(g - \dfrac{v^2}{r}\right)$

At the top the center of the circle is below the car, so $mg - N = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

Example: the car feels lighter than $mg$, and at $v = \sqrt{gr}$ the normal force drops to zero (it just leaves the road).
Watch out: at the bottom of a dip the sign flips: $N = m(g + v^2/r)$.
cards.searchQuery: car over hill crest normal force less than weight

cards.title: A car's tires have $\mu_s = 0.80$ on a flat road. What is the maximum speed on a curve of radius $50\,\mathrm{m}$, in $\mathrm{m/s}$ to 3 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$19.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$

Static friction supplies the centripetal force: $\mu_s mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $v = \sqrt{\mu_s g r} = \sqrt{(0.80)(9.8)(50)}$.

Watch out: the car's mass cancels. Heavier cars don't need a lower limit.
cards.searchQuery: maximum speed flat curve static friction mu s g r numeric

cards.title: A ball moving at $+10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is reversed by a bat and leaves at $-10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $4.0\,\mathrm{s}$ of steady change. What is its average acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$?
cards.body:
$-5.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$

$\bar a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{-10 - (+10)}{4.0}$.

Watch out: keep the signs. Using $\Delta v = 10 - 10 = 0$ is the classic error.
Tip: the sign says the acceleration points in the negative direction.
cards.searchQuery: average acceleration velocity reverses sign change in velocity

cards.title: What does the slope of a velocity-time graph represent?
cards.body:
**Acceleration.**

Slope is $\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$, which is the definition of acceleration. A horizontal line means constant velocity.

Key idea: slope of $x$-$t$ is velocity; slope of $v$-$t$ is acceleration.
cards.searchQuery: slope of velocity time graph represents acceleration

cards.title: A cart moves at $+3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $4.0\,\mathrm{s}$, then at $-2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $3.0\,\mathrm{s}$. What is its net displacement, in meters?
cards.body:
$6.0\,\mathrm{m}$

Displacement is the signed area: $(3.0)(4.0) + (-2.0)(3.0) = 12 - 6$.

Watch out: the total **distance** traveled is $12 + 6 = 18\,\mathrm{m}$, not $6.0\,\mathrm{m}$.
cards.searchQuery: displacement from velocity time graph signed area two intervals

cards.title: A ball is thrown straight up at $19.6\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and returns to its launch height. How long is it in the air, in seconds? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$4.0\,\mathrm{s}$

Set $\Delta y = 0$: $0 = v_0T - \tfrac{1}{2}gT^2$ gives $T = \dfrac{2v_0}{g} = \dfrac{2(19.6)}{9.8}$.

Why: the rise takes $v_0/g = 2.0\,\mathrm{s}$ and the fall takes the same time.
cards.searchQuery: vertical throw total time in air 2 v0 over g

cards.title: A rock is thrown straight down at $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ from a $30\,\mathrm{m}$ cliff. How fast is it moving just before impact, in $\mathrm{m/s}$ to 3 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$24.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$

Use $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2g\,h = 5.0^2 + 2(9.8)(30) = 613$, so $v = \sqrt{613}$.

Watch out: don't just add $5.0$ to the drop-only speed; the speeds don't add linearly, the squares do.
cards.searchQuery: rock thrown downward from cliff impact speed v squared equation

cards.title: A ball leaves a $20\,\mathrm{m}$ high cliff horizontally at $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How far from the base of the cliff does it land, in meters to 3 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$30.3\,\mathrm{m}$

Vertical motion sets the fall time: $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(20)}{9.8}} \approx 2.02\,\mathrm{s}$.

Why: horizontal velocity stays constant, so $x = v_0t = (15)(2.02)$.
Tip: always find the time from the vertical motion first.
cards.searchQuery: horizontal launch from cliff range fall time

cards.title: A plane heads due north at $200\,\mathrm{m/s}$ relative to the air in a $50\,\mathrm{m/s}$ wind from the west. What is its ground speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$ to 3 significant figures?
cards.body:
$206\,\mathrm{m/s}$

The two velocities are perpendicular, so $v = \sqrt{200^2 + 50^2} = \sqrt{42\,500}$.

Why: the plane's path is deflected east of north by $\tan^{-1}(50/200) \approx 14^\circ$.
Watch out: don't add the speeds ($250\,\mathrm{m/s}$); add them as vectors.
cards.searchQuery: airplane crosswind ground speed relative velocity perpendicular

cards.title: A $1500\,\mathrm{kg}$ car's engine pushes forward with $4000\,\mathrm{N}$ while resistive forces total $1000\,\mathrm{N}$. What is its acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$?
cards.body:
$2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$

Net force first: $4000 - 1000 = 3000\,\mathrm{N}$ forward. Then $a = \dfrac{\sum F}{m} = \dfrac{3000}{1500}$.

Watch out: use the **net** force, not the engine force alone.
cards.searchQuery: net force and acceleration car engine force resistive force

cards.title: In an ideal Atwood machine, $m_1 = 3.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $m_2 = 1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$. What is the magnitude of the acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$4.9\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$

$a = \dfrac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{(2.0)(9.8)}{4.0}$.

Example: the tension is $T = m_2(g + a) = (1.0)(14.7) = 14.7\,\mathrm{N}$, between $m_2g = 9.8\,\mathrm{N}$ and $m_1g = 29.4\,\mathrm{N}$.
cards.searchQuery: Atwood machine numeric 3 kg and 1 kg acceleration

cards.title: A $60\,\mathrm{kg}$ person stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating **downward** at $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. What does the scale read, in newtons? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$468\,\mathrm{N}$, less than $mg = 588\,\mathrm{N}$.

With up positive, $N - mg = m(-2.0)$, so $N = m(g - a) = (60)(9.8 - 2.0)$.

Tip: upward acceleration makes you feel heavier; downward acceleration makes you feel lighter.
cards.searchQuery: elevator accelerating downward apparent weight scale

cards.title: With quadratic drag, by what factor does the terminal speed change if the falling object's mass is multiplied by $4$ (same size and shape)?
cards.body:
It **doubles** ($\times 2$).

Terminal speed satisfies $\tfrac{1}{2}C\rho Av_t^2 = mg$, so $v_t \propto \sqrt{m}$.

Why: a heavier object needs more drag to balance its weight, so it must go faster.
cards.searchQuery: terminal speed proportional to square root of mass

cards.title: A rope lifts a $5.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ crate upward with an acceleration of $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. What is the rope's tension, in newtons? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$59\,\mathrm{N}$

With up positive, $T - mg = ma$, so $T = m(g + a) = (5.0)(9.8 + 2.0)$.

Watch out: the tension exceeds the weight ($49\,\mathrm{N}$) while the crate speeds up; it equals the weight at constant velocity.
cards.searchQuery: rope tension lifting crate upward acceleration

cards.title: For quadratic air drag $D = \tfrac{1}{2}C\rho Av^2$, by what factor does the drag force change when the speed doubles?
cards.body:
It **quadruples** ($\times 4$).

$D \propto v^2$, so doubling $v$ multiplies $D$ by $2^2 = 4$.

Example: the power needed to overcome drag, $P = Dv$, grows as $v^3$, a factor of $8$.
cards.searchQuery: quadratic drag force speed doubles factor of four
